title: Campbell’s Soup Cans
lede: Andy Warhol’s thirty-two canvases, each a single Campbell’s soup can in the same format, one for each variety the company then sold.
summary: Thirty-two identical-format paintings of soup cans, hung as a grid. Andy Warhol, 1962.

source.label: MoMA: Andy Warhol, Campbell’s Soup Cans, 1962

evidence.note: MoMA’s collection page blocks scripts, and no open image of at least 800 px was found. Description relies on Wikipedia and on the MoMA record as quoted in search results.

styles.note: The founding packaging work of American Pop: a product label repeated as a grid of flat, uniform panels. Partial fit: it has no dots or comic devices.

context: The series has 32 paintings, each showing a different variety of Campbell’s soup in a uniform 20 × 16 inch format. It was first shown in July 1962 at the Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, and the Museum of Modern Art acquired the canvases in 1996. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campbell%27s_Soup_Cans).

Wikipedia quotes MoMA that Warhol “was careful to maintain an exceptional uniformity among the canvases and to minimize the visibility of brushstrokes or other signs of his own hand.” [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campbell%27s_Soup_Cans).
In 1967 Campbell’s promoted its soup with a paper dress printed after the series: [“Souper” paper dress](ref:campbells-souper-paper-dress-1967).
interpretation: The series defines the product branch of Pop art: an everyday package isolated, enlarged, and repeated, with the hand of the painter hidden.
For a screen layout, it suggests identical cards in a strict grid in which only the label text changes.
borrow: Build a catalogue grid of identical product cards and change only the name on each card.
Keep the product front-on and centered in every cell, with no perspective or shadow.
